notes:
Direction Cosines & Ratios

  • If a line makes angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with the positive $x,y,z$ axes, its direction cosines are $l=\cos\alpha, m=\cos\beta, n=\cos\gamma$, with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
  • Direction ratios $a,b,c$ are numbers proportional to the DCs: $l=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ (similarly for $m,n$).
  • DRs of the line joining $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$: $(x_2-x_1,\ y_2-y_1,\ z_2-z_1)$; distance between them $=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2}$.

Lines

Angle between lines with DRs $(a_1,b_1,c_1)$, $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2}{\sqrt{\sum a_1^2}\sqrt{\sum a_2^2}}$
Parallel$\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}=\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$
Perpendicular$a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$
  • Cartesian equation of a line through $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ with DRs $(a,b,c)$: $\dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c}$.
  • Shortest distance between skew lines through $\vec a_1,\vec a_2$ with directions $\vec b_1,\vec b_2$: $\left|\dfrac{(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\cdot(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$; for parallel lines (common direction $\vec b$): $\left|\dfrac{\vec b\times(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)}{|\vec b|}\right|$. Two lines are coplanar (intersecting or parallel) iff this scalar triple product is $0$.

Planes

Normal form$lx+my+nz=p$ ($p$ = distance from origin, $(l,m,n)$ = DC of the normal)
Through a point, given normal $(a,b,c)$$a(x-x_1)+b(y-y_1)+c(z-z_1)=0$
Intercept form$\dfrac{x}{a}+\dfrac{y}{b}+\dfrac{z}{c}=1$ (intercepts $a,b,c$ on the axes)
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$$\dfrac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$
Angle between planes, normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_2|}$
Distance between parallel planes $ax+by+cz+d_1=0$, $ax+by+cz+d_2=0$$\dfrac{|d_1-d_2|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$

Exam tip

KCET sets 3–4 questions from this chapter, mostly plug-into-formula: angle between two lines/planes, distance of a point from a plane, and DR↔DC conversions. Always scale the coefficients of two planes to the same normal before comparing them, and remember: perpendicular → dot product zero, parallel → ratios equal.

For two skew lines with direction vectors $\vec b_1,\vec b_2$ passing through points with position vectors $\vec a_1,\vec a_2$, the shortest distance between them is
options: $\left|\dfrac{(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\cdot(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$
$\left|\dfrac{(\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2)(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$
questions.explanation: This is the standard vector formula for the shortest distance between two skew lines.

questions.q: A line makes an angle of $90^\circ$ with the $x$-axis and $60^\circ$ with the $y$-axis. The angle it makes with the $z$-axis is
questions.explanation: $\cos^2 90^\circ + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \Rightarrow 0 + 0.25 + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \Rightarrow \cos\gamma = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \Rightarrow \gamma = 30^\circ$.

questions.explanation: With $\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(3,-1,-3)$, the scalar triple product with $(2,3,4)$ and $(5,2,1)$ equals $0$, so the lines are coplanar; since their direction ratios are not proportional, they intersect (rather than being parallel).

questions.explanation: The normal to the plane is $(3,-6,2)$. Since $(2)(3)+(3)(-6)+(6)(2)=6-18+12=0$, the line's direction is perpendicular to the normal, so the line is parallel to the plane.

questions.q: The plane through the line of intersection of $x+y+z=1$ and $2x+3y-z=4$, passing through the origin, is
questions.explanation: The family is $(x+y+z-1)+\lambda(2x+3y-z-4)=0$. Through the origin: $-1-4\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-\tfrac14$, giving $2x+y+5z=0$ after simplifying.
